source: Superposition and Interference
Overlapping waves add point by point: crest on crest builds up, crest on trough cancels.
Students think two waves that cancel are destroyed, rather than passing through each other unchanged.
When two waves meet in the same medium, what happens? With the wave graphs you can follow it point by point: the displacements simply add.

Superposition: where waves overlap, the total displacement is the sum of the separate displacements. Crest on crest builds up (constructive interference); crest on trough cancels (destructive interference). Afterward, each wave goes on unchanged.
Two pulses (dashed) and their sum (solid). They pass through each other and come out as they went in.

Why add? For small displacements, the force restoring each bit of string is proportional to how far it is displaced, so the equation of motion is linear: if each wave alone is a solution, their sum is a solution too. Nothing in the medium "remembers" which wave a bit of motion came from. Noise-canceling headphones use this: a microphone picks up the noise, and the speaker adds a copy turned upside down, so crest meets trough at your ear.

Thinking two waves that cancel are destroyed. At the instant two opposite pulses overlap exactly, the string is flat, but it is moving fast: the energy is all kinetic for that moment. A moment later both pulses re-emerge, unchanged. Check: energy cannot vanish, so the waves must still be there.
A pulse $3.0\ \text{cm}$ high meets a pulse $2.0\ \text{cm}$ deep (upside down) from the other direction. What is the displacement where they overlap exactly? What are they like afterward?
Adding pulses
$1.0\ \text{cm}$ while they overlap; unchanged afterward
Add with signs: $3.0 + (-2.0) = 1.0\ \text{cm}$.
Afterward each continues unchanged: $3.0\ \text{cm}$ up and $2.0\ \text{cm}$ down, moving apart.
Two speakers play the same $343\ \text{Hz}$ tone in step. You stand $4.0\ \text{m}$ from one and $5.5\ \text{m}$ from the other. Is the sound loud or quiet? ($v = 343\ \text{m/s}$.)
Two speakers
Quiet (destructive interference)
Wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{343}{343} = 1.00\ \text{m}$.
Path difference: $5.5 - 4.0 = 1.5\ \text{m} = 1.5\lambda$.
A half-number of wavelengths means crest meets trough: destructive.
Whole numbers of wavelengths ($0, \lambda, 2\lambda, \dots$) would be constructive.
